system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-07-21 06:05:00 to 2154-07-22 12:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and chest pressure following her recent bilateral nephrectomy. She was found to be in atrial flutter with a rapid ventricular rate, and imaging revealed new bilateral pleural effusions and possible pericardial effusion. An echocardiogram showed a reduced ejection fraction of 29%, consistent with acute on chronic systolic heart failure, likely exacerbated by tachycardia. She underwent hemodialysis with ultrafiltration, resulting in significant symptom improvement. A transesophageal echocardiogram ruled out intracardiac clots, and successful cardioversion restored sinus rhythm. Her warfarin dose was adjusted due to a subtherapeutic INR on admission, and she was transitioned from atenolol to metoprolol for better rate control. Amlodipine was discontinued due to well-controlled blood pressure. She remained afebrile without diarrhea, and her C. diff treatment was continued. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged for cardiology and infectious disease.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Intestinal infection due to Clostridium difficile
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other parts of uterus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago. I couldn’t lie flat and felt like I had to burp, but it was more in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds uncomfortable. Was it similar to past episodes when your heart rhythm was off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like that. But this time it lasted longer, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. I see you missed your dialysis yesterday because of the holiday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I knew I’d feel a bit puffy, but I didn’t expect this much trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That likely contributed. Fluid builds up when you miss dialysis, and with your heart condition, it can cause shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on amiodarone and metoprolol since my last episode. Is my heart rhythm okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your EKG shows you’re in normal sinus rhythm. No atrial fibrillation right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the chest pressure then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s due to heart failure worsening from fluid overload and your mitral valve leak. Your ejection fraction is around 40-45%, which is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Your troponin is normal, and the EKG doesn’t show ischemia. It’s more likely decompensated heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my potassium? I remember it was high in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 6.9 on admission — quite high. But you didn’t have EKG changes, so we gave calcium, insulin, and sugar to shift it into cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll recheck after dialysis. It should come down once we remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows small pleural effusions and some atelectasis at the bases — consistent with fluid overload, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that clear up with dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as we remove fluid, your lungs should improve. You’ll have dialysis today around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also felt lightheaded earlier. Is that from my heart rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was 52, and you mentioned dizziness. We’re lowering your metoprolol from 50mg twice daily to 37.5mg to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been trying to cut back with my cardiologist anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also held your warfarin. Your INR was 4.6 — too high, increases bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 3mg, but they changed it to 2mg in the ER. Should I stay on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it held today. Before discharge, we’ll check your INR again and restart at a safe dose, likely 2mg daily if it’s below 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can breathe easier already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We removed about 3 liters — that should help your heart work better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show potassium is now 4.6 — perfect. Creatinine and urea are also down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the dialysis really helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it corrected the potassium and reduced fluid. Your breathing and chest pressure should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about my mitral valve? It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s moderate to severe, and we discussed it with your cardiologist. For now, we’ll manage it medically. Surgery isn’t urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart failure — anything new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend starting an ACE inhibitor after discharge to help your heart function long-term. Discuss it with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8 — safe to restart warfarin at 2mg daily. We’ll send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue amiodarone, levothyroxine, sevelamer, and aspirin. We’re cutting omeprazole in half and reducing midodrine to 10mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 37.5mg twice daily — that’s one and a half of the 25mg tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting. Keep monitoring your weight and symptoms. Call if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your cardiologist in a week. They may want a heart monitor to check for silent arrhythmias.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’re discharging you home in stable condition. Keep up with dialysis and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check — you’re still feeling well, no chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I watch for bleeding with the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially in the first few days. Report any unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or dark stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll check my INR as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are signed. A nurse will go over instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay on schedule with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for shortness of breath and chest discomfort following a missed dialysis session. She had a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, systolic dysfunction, and mitral regurgitation. On admission, she was in normal sinus rhythm but had fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and a supratherapeutic INR. A chest X-ray showed small bilateral pleural effusions and bibasilar atelectasis. She underwent hemodialysis, which resolved her symptoms and normalized her potassium. Her metoprolol dose was reduced due to bradycardia and lightheadedness, and warfarin was held due to elevated INR, with plans to restart at 2mg daily. She was discharged home in stable condition with medication adjustments and follow-up arranged with cardiology.
